summary: This document describes the SIP event package kpml, which monitors DTMF key presses using XML documents called Key Press Markup Language. A SUBSCRIBE carries filters for which key presses to capture, and NOTIFY messages report them to an application server. It is for supplemental or mid-call key presses.

eli5.summary: When you press phone buttons during a call, a computer might need to know. This lets the computer say which buttons it cares about and get told when you press them.

questions: sip dtmf key press event package
how does sip report dtmf key presses
subtitle: How an application server subscribes over SIP to be told about specific phone key presses, using small XML filters.

tldr.problem: An application may need to know about a few key presses during a call, but asking for every keystroke is wasteful, and routing the media through a media server just to hear tones is clumsy.
tldr.mechanism: A SIP SUBSCRIBE carries a KPML request listing digit patterns written in DRegex. The user device or gateway answers with NOTIFY messages carrying a KPML response only when the patterns match, or when a timer or error occurs.
tldr.outcome: Applications get only the digits they care about, with optional digit suppression, timers and buffering. Because the digits can be sensitive, subscriptions must be authenticated.

today: RFC 4730 is a Proposed Standard from November 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Reporting Key Presses Over SIP
sections.content:
RFC 4730 defines the SIP event package kpml. It lets "dumb phones" and the gateways that receive their signals report user key presses, often called "digit reporting" or DTMF reporting. The filters and reports are XML documents in the Key Press Markup Language (KPML).

Its scope is collecting supplemental key presses or mid-call key presses (triggers). It removes the need for "hair-pinning" media through a Media Server, or for duplicating all the DTMF events, when an Application Server wants to trigger service processing on digit patterns.

RFC 2833 packets can carry telephone events point to point in an RTP stream, but protocol translation and complex call control need more. An application could ask for every key press, yet most only care about one or a few, so the user interface needs a way to be told what to look for. A stated goal is a very small memory and processing footprint.
sections.eli5: Some phones cannot show screens or menus, only buttons. This gives a computer a way to ask, "tell me when someone presses these buttons," without listening to everything.

sections.title: How a Subscription Works
sections.content:
An application builds an application/kpml-request+xml document with the digit patterns it wants and puts it in a SIP SUBSCRIBE. The request is routed to the user interface with standard SIP routing, and KPML subscriptions do not fork. The body identifies the target media stream by referencing the dialog identifiers of the session that carries it.

Once established, the user interface sends application/kpml-response+xml documents in NOTIFY requests when digits are collected or when timeouts or errors occur.

A subscription is either one-shot, which ends after the first match and a report, or persistent. Persistent ones are persist (a NOTIFY on every match) or single-notify (one NOTIFY, then silence until the application issues a new request on the dialog). The single-notify mode supports lock-step, race-free handling of user input between different digit maps. A persistent subscription can also be ended by replacing the request, sending a null document, or sending SUBSCRIBE with an expires value of zero.

The default subscription duration is 7200 seconds. The event package name is kpml, and the three package parameters call-id, remote-tag and local-tag identify the dialog being monitored.
sections.eli5: The computer sends the phone a short list of patterns, like "tell me about 1-2-3". The phone watches the buttons and sends a note back when the pattern shows up. For a one-shot request it stops after the first note.

sections.title: Patterns, Timers and Buffering
sections.content:
A request holds a pattern element with one or more regex elements. The matcher takes the longest match, as in H.248.1. If several expressions match with equal length, the first in document order wins. A tag attribute on a regex is returned in the report so the application knows which one matched.

Three timers, set as attributes of pattern in milliseconds, control waiting. interdigittimer (default 4000) is the longest wait between digits. criticaldigittimer (default 1000) applies when the digits so far match one pattern but a longer one could still match. extradigittimer (default 500) applies after the longest match, so an enterkey can be collected. The enterkey attribute names a string, such as the pound key, that ends a pattern at once.

Long key presses use the L modifier, for example a long pound key written as L#. The long attribute sets what counts as long, defaulting to 2500 milliseconds.

The user interface MUST buffer user input from the moment it accepts an authenticated subscription, and MUST NOT hand a subscriber digits detected before that subscriber was authenticated and authorized. A flush element of yes discards earlier input. A key press that cannot match any pattern is discarded together with everything buffered before it. If the interface drops old digits, it sets forced_flush to true.

With nopartial set to true, only complete matches are reported.
sections.eli5: The phone is like a careful listener with three egg timers: one for how long to wait between button presses, and others for deciding if a longer pattern might still be coming. It also remembers recent button presses so a new request can look back at them.

sections.title: DRegex and Digit Suppression
sections.content:
DRegex is a telephony-oriented mapping of POSIX Extended Regular Expressions. It differs on purpose: the star character is the star key, a dot means repetition, x is any digit 0-9, and there is no alternation operator |. Alternatives are instead written as multiple regex elements. White space is removed before parsing.

Examples from the RFC: x{10} is ten digits, 011x{7,15} is 011 followed by seven to fifteen digits, and *6[179#] matches star-6 followed by 1, 7, 9 or pound. The characters are digits 0-9, star, pound, R and A through D. Negation inside a character class applies only to digits.

By default the user interface passes tones in-band (RFC 2833 packets or actual tones) in parallel with reporting, so called applications are not broken. A pre element inside a regex asks for suppression: once the input matches the pre part, further input is held back. A report carries suppressed="true" if it did suppress. Suppression is optional (MAY). An interface that cannot do it sets suppressed to false and matches the concatenated pre plus value pattern.

Suppression holds digits back from the far end. The RFC warns that a sensible inter-digit timer is critical, because an errant dot could suppress digit sending forever.
sections.eli5: DRegex is a tiny secret code for describing button patterns, like "seven numbers" or "star then six". Suppression is like the phone saying, "I will keep these button presses to myself instead of passing them along."

sections.title: Reports and Status Codes
sections.content:
A KPML report has two mandatory attributes, code and text. A match gives code 200 and text OK, plus the matched digits in the digit attribute, using the star and pound characters. KPML status codes are separate from SIP result codes: a SUBSCRIBE can succeed in SIP while the NOTIFY carries a KPML error. Clients MUST handle unknown codes by looking at the first digit only, and MUST NOT interpret the text.

The immediate NOTIFY after a SUBSCRIBE has no KPML body unless buffered input already matches, or an error occurred. A NOTIFY with no body just means the subscription succeeded.

Notification is rate limited. The user interface MUST NOT send messages faster than 25 per second, one every 40 milliseconds, and the sustained rate shall be no more than 100 Notifies per minute. The RFC strongly recommends against using KPML for digit-by-digit messaging, and notifications should travel over a congestion-controlled transport such as TCP.
sections.eli5: Each note back has a number saying how things went. Like a teacher's stamp, "200" means all good, and the number groups tell you whether the trouble was the typing or the request itself.

sections.title: Protecting Sensitive Digits
sections.content:
Key presses may be calling card or credit card numbers, so the notifier MUST authenticate the requesting party before accepting a subscription. User interfaces MUST implement SIP Digest authentication, the sips: scheme and TLS. Subscribers SHOULD use sips: and MAY use S/MIME on the content.

The default authorization allows a subscriber who authenticates with a specific identity to monitor sessions in which the same or an equivalent authenticated identity takes part. A notifier MAY also be configured with a list of trusted subscribers, such as application servers in the same domain.

A user interface MUST NOT downgrade its own security policy. If its policy requires authenticated, authorized subscribers over secure channels, it must reject others. The RFC also warns that eavesdroppers could read unencrypted digits and attackers could inject fake notifications. Because KPML is XML, the security considerations of RFC 3023 and RFC 3406 MUST be met.
sections.eli5: Button presses can include secrets like card numbers. So the phone checks who is asking, and only tells people who are allowed to hear.

sections.title: Where This Fits in SIP
sections.content:
KPML builds on SIP events. It uses RFC 3265 SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY and the dialog identifiers of RFC 3261. The RFC also gives example documents, for instance monitoring for the octothorpe, collecting a dial string, and call flows with supplemental digits and multiple applications.

By default the monitored stream is the one coming from the user interface itself. An optional stream element with the value reverse monitors key presses arriving from the remote user agent instead, as in the media proxy case. Several subscriptions may exist at once on different dialogs or on one dialog with different event ids, but a device that cannot support that must return status 533.

Forked requests are NOT ALLOWED for this package, and implementers MUST NOT define state agents or allow subscriptions to resource lists.
sections.eli5: It rides on the same mail system SIP already uses for calls, so a phone system does not need a whole new channel just to report button presses.
